title: The Dormition
hook: the Orthodox call the August feast of Mary her falling asleep
tomorrow: Mary close: do whatever he tells you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary and Protestants: one song, sung at dusk in more than one church. Your line was she belongs to all. What did you find you share? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

Look closely at the icon. Mary lies on a low bed, eyes closed, hands folded. Around her stand the apostles, bent with grief. One leans down close to her face. Others hold their hands to their cheeks. And behind the bed, taller than everyone, stands Christ, in light. In his arms he holds a small figure, wrapped in white, like a newborn. That small figure is Mary's soul. Now think back to the icons of Christmas: a mother holding her swaddled child. Here it's turned around. The son holds his mother, swaddled, and carries her home. Orthodox Christians have a name for this feast, and it isn't death. Today's word.
screen: `MARY ON A LOW BED, APOSTLES GRIEVING.` → `CHRIST HOLDS A SMALL SWADDLED FIGURE.` → `THE SON CARRIES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Koimesis, the falling asleep. In Latin, Dormition. It is the feast the Latin Church calls the Assumption, and Eastern Catholics keep it as the Dormition too. Second, why sleep. The New Testament uses that word for the death of the faithful. When Stephen is stoned, the Douay-Rheims says that, having prayed for the men killing him, "he fell asleep in the Lord." Paul writes to the Thessalonians about those who are asleep, so that they won't grieve like people without hope. You only call it sleep if you expect a waking. Third, the story. The Bible itself doesn't tell how Mary's life ended. Tradition does: it says the apostles were gathered to her bedside, and that she was laid in a tomb, and that her body was not left there. The icon you just saw comes from that tradition, not from a Gospel, and the Church keeps the two apart. Fourth, two names for one hope. The Catholic Church teaches, as dogma, that Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Notice how it's phrased. Pius the Twelfth defined the Assumption without deciding whether she died first. The Catechism itself quotes an Eastern hymn about her falling asleep. The Orthodox speak plainly of her death, her falling asleep, and of her son taking her to himself. One tradition names the arrival, the other names the moment of closing her eyes. Both are pointing at the same door.
screen: `KOIMESIS: THE FALLING ASLEEP.` · `HE FELL ASLEEP IN THE LORD.` · `THE STORY COMES FROM TRADITION.` · `ONE HOPE, TWO NAMES.` · then, large: `TAKEN UP, BODY AND SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with Orthodox Christians. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, or an Orthodox Christian you know, or simply the candles lit in front of icons tonight. Hold them for a few breaths, with good will. If you pray, you can use a short refrain from Byzantine services: most holy Mother of God, save us. Say it slowly, on the out-breath, once for them and once for yourself. If you don't pray, simply hold the picture of the icon: a son carrying his mother, gently, the way she once carried him. The bell holds the time.
Dormition. The falling asleep: the Eastern name for the end of Mary's earthly life, the feast the West calls the Assumption. Today's word.
Your line: fell asleep. Today, when you think of someone you've lost, try the old word for it once: not gone, but asleep, waiting for morning. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians keep the feast of the Dormition with the Divine Liturgy and a fast beforehand; in the West, Catholics keep the same day as the Assumption, which in some countries is a holy day of obligation.

notes: The index hook names the date (15 August); per the claims rule the voice says 'the same summer day the Latin Church keeps the Assumption' and the script hook field drops the date. Confirm. Some Orthodox churches keep the feast on the Julian calendar, which falls on a different civil date; 'the same day' is left unqualified. A Keeper may want 'the same day on the church calendar'.
Confirm Douay-Rheims Acts 7:59 ends 'he fell asleep in the Lord' (KJV 7:60 has 'he fell asleep').

Munificentissimus Deus paraphrased: 'having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory', and the point that it does not decide whether she died. The voice adds that CCC 966 quotes an Eastern hymn (the Byzantine troparion of the Dormition) about her falling asleep; confirm.
The icon description (Christ holding Mary's soul as a swaddled infant, reversing the Nativity) is the standard Dormition type; confirm.
Pius the Twelfth named as the pope who defined the Assumption, without a year.
